story_text.value:
I’ve recently moved over to macOS this summer and previously I heavily used Linux (still do as I have a homeserver running Arch and Omarchy Thinkpad for fun). I have a few LUKS Encrypted hard drives with photos I wanted on my Mac and then quickly realized that there’s no native way to open the drive.

So I spent some time to make luksmith, essentially decrypting the luks drive, mounting the underlying EXT4 drive and using Apple’s Userland FSKit Library to make it appear in the finder window to make it as close to home on a Mac as I can (with journaling caveats because I can’t control which order writes happen in).

It’s completely free to read and copy files from the drive if you try it out ‘brew install --cask betizzel/luksmith/luksmac’. And $9.99 one time purchase to unlock writing to the drive. No account needed, no telemetry shared back to me, no network connections made.

Requires Apple Silicon + macOS 26. Full format support and limitations here: [https://luksmith.app/#formats](https://luksmith.app/#formats)

available on the appstore: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/luksmith/id6806869711?mt=12

and the website: https://luksmith.app/#formats

title.value: Show HN: Luksmith – Mount LUKS Ext4 Drives Natively in Finder on Apple Silicon

story_text.value:
I'm a 47yo full stack developer that's investing all his free time (and not only that) into thinkering, building, researching with AI. Some days ago I found a paper about distilling kokoro on a ~9MB with around 25x RTF. It was very interesting and since the experiment was on a single english voice and I'm Italian, I wanted to see if I could manage to distill it in my language but the training recipe wasn't replicable. So I spent some days researching, experimenting and found the why and even some more tweaks to improve the overall result. The demo I linked shows you how close it is to the original kokoro and you can play straight in the browser (If you use the package locally it's faster)

Paper: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23400040 Code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/MithrilMan/teacher-in-the-loop Weights: https://huggingface.co/MithrilMan/teacher-in-the-loop

pip install teacher-in-the-loop

P.S. I wanted to publish the paper on arXiv but I need to be endorsed, would be nice if anyone that can help me could endorse me arxiv.org/auth/endorse?x=GPI7BZ Honestly would be just to be added to the hf papers, I don't seek fame nor fortune lol

story_text.value:
Endo is a Higher-Order Harness (HOH).

From the easiest concept to understand to the more complex ones, Endo gives you: * A single, simple UI to use any agent provider with your existing subscriptions, and hot-swap agents right in the middle of a session. * An orchestration layer, which I call HOH, allowing arbitrary composition of agents to achieve any workflow. A fun case I tried was asking Fable and Astra to mock a presidential debate. * An agent protocol that abstracts any agent. The key insight here is that every LLM is an agent—instead of treating the LLM as just one node inside an external ReAct loop.

Endo was a concept formed while I was building OpenChart (https://github.com/longsurf-ai/openchart). To power trading workflows, I needed to support scenarios where strict determinism is required, while still keeping the flexibility of an agent's inference-time decision-making capability. A new form factor was needed between rigid n8n-style workflows and open-ended ReAct loop agents.

Thus the creation of Endo. Endo is short for Endomorphism, a term rooted in category theory and functional programming. An endomorphism is a function that transforms an object into another object of the same type. Similarly, Endo itself is built purely on functional programming principles, relying heavily on Effect (https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect).

..And if you have patience to speak technical jargons, Endo is: * An agent orchestration layer—Higher-Order Harness (HOH)—where an entire agent is treated the same as a single LLM call, enabling arbitrary composition of extremely complex workflows. * A way to abstract any harness into a standardized protocol, where raw models and agents behave the exact same way, in a KV-cache-friendly manner. * A workflow engine that enables arbitrary composition of agents with a single workflow language.

It's completely open source, and if you think this idea is cool, let's build together. Just for the fun of it.

story_text.value:
when I started using coding agents heavily, they began creating tons of Git worktrees. different tools like Codex, Claude Code, T3 Code, Orca, Superset, and others all put their worktrees in different directories, which made them pretty hard to find.

I know you can just ask an agent to find them, and a lot of people do exactly that. but I wanted a deterministic solution that wouldn't depend on an agent getting things right or waste extra tokens.

so.. I built Lopper!

it's a tool that searches for git repositories and worktrees across different directories on your machine and shows them all in one place in a TUI, where you can inspect them and remove the ones you no longer need. it also has a CLI for scripts and agents, so they can manage worktrees more reliably.

would you use something like this? what am I missing compared to just asking an agent to handle it?

story_text.value:
When Apple left Clozure Common Lisp behind by switching to Apple Silicon, I started kicking around the idea of building my own Lisp/Objective-C bridge by combining Apple Documentation, the clang AST, and introspection of the Objective-C runtime.

There was a CCL porting effort, but I really wanted to use SBCL anyway.

Truth be told — what I really wanted was a 21st-century CLIM variant on top of modern AppKit 26. So I let that idea rattle around in my skull for a while — and eventually it bounced up against the memory of Ck (Curses-based Tk).

Anybody remember that?

I liked Tcl/Tk and [incr Tcl] and it had always stuck in my head how great an idea it was to have something along the lines of CLIM for regular terminals as well as GUI.

So anyway, I stumbled upon the open-source CLIM2 source still maintained by Franz, and the wheels commenced to turn.

Oh yeah, and my very first programming environment had been Turbo Pascal. That integrated debugger was really something.

And y'know, it all started to come together as an idea about modernizing CLIM and modifying Portable Hemlock to run on top of it — and integrating a Debugger with conditional breakpoints and Step In/Step Out/Step Over, CLIM presentations, Inspector...

And in years past, I'd have just dreamed about it.

But the past three years have been crazy. GPT4 was the first time I seriously tried to build things with an LLM. And I've been pushing the LLMs as far as they would go to build my intuition mainly.

But up until this year they've been mostly crap.

I used "Build Common Lisp" as my north star because the Dietz ANSI tests seemed like a nearly perfect product specification.

Long story short: I threw away 7 attempts before I won ANSI — https://gitlab.com/patchwork1-ai/whateverlisp — and while I was waiting for Claude and Codex to grovel through ANSI I was trying my hand at my grand idea of Turbo Lisp.

Side note: my high score on ANSI is 21,916/21,925 passing (99.96%); 21,925 executed; 9 failing. And those 9? Yeah I don't think you could pass those without failing 30+ other ones.

So anyway — It’s called *Turbo Lisp* (based on SBCL). It brings together a Listener, debugger, object inspector, conditional breakpoints + stepper, and Zeta—a variant of Portable Hemlock that uses WhateverCLIM as its front-end.

On macOS, it uses native AppKit UI through *Chattanooga, a Lisp/Objective-C bridge I built*. It also runs in the terminal through *Oak Ridge, my Lisp port of Ratatui*. Both use *WhateverCLIM*, which is the CLIM2 code from Franz plus my own modernization, including *presentations*: displayed Lisp objects you can click and inspect.

*v0.2.1 patch release* is available for Apple Silicon Macs, Intel Macs, and Linux x86-64. The Mac builds currently require macOS 26.

I’m especially interested in hearing:

* Does it install and start properly on your machine? * Can you find your way around the Listener, editor, and debugger? * Does the terminal interface work with your terminal emulator? * Where does it feel confusing, awkward, or broken?

A report that says “I tried this and got stuck here” is useful. Please include your OS, CPU architecture, and terminal emulator where relevant.

It’s still early, and I’m looking for honest feedback from people using it outside my own setup.

title.value: Show HN: Turbo Lisp – A Common Lisp IDE for macOS and the Terminal

story_text.value:
The official openai/math repo is closed to issues, PRs, and discussion.

I made this app to share some explanatory videos that help us all make sense of the release, catalogue follow-ons and improvements that build on the openai research, and more broadly provide a set of community tools for distributed research.

I am not a trained mathematician and most of the math exceeds my understanding. As such, the videos _are_ AI-generated, but IMHO, go a long ways towards helping folks like me understand the problems, proofs, and related ideas.

Suggestions are welcome.

story_text.value:
TL;DR: 12 years ago I built a service that forwards simple HTML forms to an email address. I've been procrastinating on finishing it ever since, until today. You point your form at it and every submission lands in your inbox. It runs on credits, 1 credit = 1 message, no subscription. Perfect for static websites.

—

Hey folks, back around 2014, alongside my job as a software engineer, I was building a lot of static websites for my own clients, mostly small businesses that just wanted a simple site. To avoid headaches, I went fully static, often hosted on GitHub Pages and similar.

But most clients also wanted a contact form, and a form needs a server running somewhere. I had my own weekend-hacked service for this, which literally just forwarded the form to the client's email.

I didn't invent anything here: one service I particularly remember was FormKeep by thoughtbot, that I really liked.

So I started building my own, mostly because I loved losing myself in side projects like this, and also because I was a cheap ass and thought I could do something similar for less, and without a subscription.

By 2016 I had done about 90% of what I'm showing you today. I called it "The Great Forwarder". Everything was ready: backend, frontend, hosting, Stripe, landing page. I even had a designer friend help with the design (sorry, Valentin, if I've botched it since). Then I started another project, which took off right away and took all my attention for a while. Fun fact: that project has been using this service ever since, and almost every message ever sent through it came from there.

So for years, I kept Forwarder.cc up to date, upgrading libraries and trying new ones: axios, got, Redux, Zustand, create-react-app, webpack, Vite… It became my laboratory for everything I wanted to explore, while always staying up and maintained (again, for my own use only).

The only thing that ever held me back from launching it was a missing help center, and, more honestly, the fear of putting it in front of people.

So today's the day: after 12 years of procrastination, I finally finished the help center.

I know there are a ton of similar services nowadays, but anyway, what do you think of that help center?

title.value: Show HN: Forwarder.cc – Static-site forms sent to your inbox, pay per message
